analytic.title: A Comprehensive Study on Execution Right Delegation Scheduling Algorithm for Multiprocessors

div.p: In scheduling algorithms based on the Rate Monotonic method, tasks with shorter periods have higher priorities, whereas those with longer periods tend to suffer from increased response times and jitters. To address this issue, we previously proposed the Execution Right Delegation (ERD) scheduling algorithm, which introduces a high-priority server for privileged tasks. While our earlier work demonstrated the feasibility of ERD with a single privileged task on a small-scale multiprocessor system, the approach remained limited in scope. In this paper, we present a comprehensive study of the ERD scheduling algorithm for multiprocessors. We extend the algorithm to support an arbitrary number of privileged tasks, up to the number of available processors, thereby generalizing the original framework. Furthermore, we conduct an extensive experimental evaluation on systems with up to 32 processors, examining response times, jitters, and schedulability under diverse workloads. The results show that the extended ERD algorithm improves the response times of privileged tasks compared with conventional partitioned Fixed-Task-Priority scheduling, while also revealing trade-offs in jitter characteristics.

div.head: I. INTRODUCTION
div.p: Real-time scheduling algorithms aim to determine feasible schedules for periodic tasks with parameters such as execution times and deadlines. In multiprocessor systems, two primary categories of scheduling have been studied: partitioned scheduling, in which tasks are statically allocated to specific processors, and global scheduling, in which tasks are dynamically dispatched from a shared ready queue. Partitioned scheduling requires solving the task-to-processor assignment problem, which is known to be NP-hard, while global scheduling allows unrestricted migration but often suffers from poor scalability. As a result, several techniques have been proposed to improve processor utilization and schedulability in multiprocessor systems.

In addition to meeting deadlines, real-time scheduling must also provide predictable response times for important tasks. For uniprocessor systems, we previously proposed the Execution Right Delegation (ERD) [1] method, which introduces a high-priority server for a privileged task that would otherwise have lower priority under the Rate Monotonic (RM) [2] policy. Such tasks are motivated by applications where urgent notifications may have longer periods than control messages, such as in automotive communication systems (e.g., CAN messages) or embedded factory automation systems.

In our earlier works, we introduced mERD, a multiprocessor version of ERD, under a partitioned model where only privileged tasks are allowed to migrate. At MCSoC 2021, we presented the initial design with a single privileged task on a dual-processor platform [3]. Later, in 2023, we further extended mERD to support two privileged tasks and evaluated its behavior on systems with up to eight processors [4]. Although these studies demonstrated the advantages of mERD scheduling, their scope remained limited in terms of the number of privileged tasks and the scale of experimental evaluation.

In this paper, we present a comprehensive study of the mERD scheduling algorithm. We generalize the algorithm to support an arbitrary number of privileged tasks, up to the number of available processors, thereby removing the restrictions of our previous work. We also perform an extensive evaluation on systems with up to 32 processors, examining worst-case response times (WCRT), jitter, and schedulability across a wide range of workloads. This study confirms the effectiveness of the extended mERD algorithm for privileged tasks and reveals inherent trade-offs in jitter behavior.

The organization of this paper is as follows. Section II describes background of our study. Section III describes related work in terms of real-time scheduling algorithms. Section IV shows the algorithm of the ERD method for uniprocessor systems. Section V proposes the extended mERD. Evaluation of the proposed method is shown in Section VI. Finally, Section VII concludes the paper.

div.head: II. BACKGROUND
div.p: A task set is denoted as Γ = {τ 1 , τ 2 , ..., τ n }, where each task τ i is characterized by a tuple (C i , T i , D i , π i ). Here, C i represents the worst-case execution time, T i the period (or minimum inter-arrival time), D i the relative deadline (D i ≤ T i ), and π i the static priority of the task. The priority assigment follow either the RM or Deadline Monotonic (DM) [5] rule. A task releases an infinite sequence of Jobs. Once Job is released, it runs during the defined time C i . Job is released every period T i . A deadline miss occurs if Job does not finish by its deadline D i .

div.head: III. RELATED WORK
div.p: Real-time scheduling on multiprocessor systems has been extensively studied in the last two decades. Existing approaches are commonly classified into partitioned, global, and semi-partitioned schemes [6]. Partitioned scheduling statically assigns each task to a processor and schedules tasks independently within each processor and is better suited for hard real-time systems [7]. This approach offers predictability and implementation simplicity but suffers from NP-hard task assignment problems due to bin-packing complexity [8] [9] [10] [11]. In contrast, global scheduling allows all tasks to migrate freely among processors, offering higher flexibility but often leading to larger migration overheads and reduced cache efficiency [6] [12].

Semi-partitioned scheduling was introduced to combine the advantages of both approaches. In this scheme, most tasks are statically assigned, while a limited subset is allowed to migrate under specific rules. Several semi-partitioned algorithms have been proposed [13], such as restricted migration EDF [14], dynamic partitioning EDF [15], and adaptive partitioned EDF [16]. These studies demonstrated improved schedulability compared with purely partitioned scheduling. However, most semi-partitioned algorithms rely on EDF-based dynamic priorities and do not consider the fixed-priority task model widely used in industrial systems.

In fixed-priority scheduling, several server-based methods have been proposed to reduce the response time of specific tasks. The Deferrable Server and Priority Exchange (PE) [17] are classic techniques that improve responsiveness by temporarily modifying priority assignments and execution budgets. Our previous work, ERD, extended this idea for uniprocessor systems by introducing a virtual server for a privileged task.

Recent research trends also explore new perspectives on multiprocessor scheduling. Reachability-based response-time analysis under release jitter for global fixed-priority systems [18], and LP-based response-time bounds for uniform multiprocessors [19], have advanced theoretical analysis in global scheduling. In addition, semi-partitioned scheduling in ROS2 executor models [20] and flexible resource-access protocols [21] have drawn attention for practical applications. In contrast to these studies, our work focuses on a fixed-priority, serverbased semi-partitioned scheduling scheme. mERD restricts migration to privileged tasks and introduces per-processor primary and secondary servers to improve their responsiveness.

div.head: A. Overview of ERD
div.p: The ERD method aims to reduce the response time and jitter of a privileged task τ p within a task set. It introduces a highpriority virtual server (VS) characterized by a capacity C s , period T s and static priority π s ensuring that all task deadlines in the set remain satisfied. The privileged task τ p is assumed to have a relatively low priority due to its long period or deadline. By assigning the VS a high priority, τ p can be executed at an elevated priority level while consuming the server capacity C s . The behavior of the VS is derived from the PE model. The theorems and a lemmas underlying ERD is described in [1].
Definition 1 (Response Time Analysis (RTA) [22]). In a fixedpriority scheduling, the longest response time i , R i , of task τ i is computed as:

div.p: Definition 2 (Delegation of Execution Right). In ERD method, VS is scheduled based on RM rule. When VS is given the execution right, a privileged task τ p is executed instead of VS. This situation is called Delegation of Execution Right. If a job of τ p has already finished when the execution right is available, the behavior follows PE rule [17] where jobs of the other tasks are executed while the server capacity is accumulated at the priority level of the running job.

div.head: A. Overview of mERD
div.p: The mERD is based on a partitioned schedule, where only privileged tasks can be migrated. Therefore, it falls under the category of semi-partitioned scheduling, which is defined in [6]. mERD is a scheduling algorithm but not a partitioning algorithm. The premise of mERD is that tasks are assigned to each processor statically before scheduling, i.e., partitioning is already done in advance.

In the extended mERD, each processor maintains at most one primary server and one secondary server. The primary server follows the same rules as in uniprocessor ERD, serving the privileged task originally assigned to the processor. The secondary server may execute privileged tasks migrated from other processors. It is established only when the task set assigned to the processor provides slack time, and it is designed to operate without compromising the schedulability guarantees of higher-priority servers on the same processor. A secondary server can accept multiple privileged tasks during execution, but at most one task is executed at a time. div.p: Each processor has at most one primary server and one secondary server.

div.head: C. Implementation
div.p: In the uniprocessor ERD, V S is scheduled as a task based on RM rule. When V S has the execution right, τ p is executed instead of it. In mERD, each processor P i has its primary server V S i and secondary server sV S i which are scheduled in the same way as uniprocessor ERD. Each processor may have one privileged task, denoted as τ pi , in mERD. When V S i obtains the execution right, the privileged task τ pi originally assigned to V S i consumes the capacity of V S i in the same manner as in the uniprocessor ERD. When sV S i obtains the execution right, another privileged task τ pj (j ̸ = i) may migrate from P j to P i and consume the capacity of sV S i . In this case, P i temporarily holds τ pj as a guest task.

Algorithm 1 shows the pseudocode of the mERD scheduling steps. In the algorithm, scheds represents a list (or array) of schedulers, one for each processor P i . From lines 1 to 3, once the scheduler of P i is obtained, it performs scheduling in the same manner as the single-processor ERD algorithm. If the processor has a guest task in either rdy_q or slp_q, the task is returned to its originally assigned processor (lines 4-13). The decision on task migration is made at every scheduling period (or tick). When a candidate scheduler (i.e., processor) is available, a privileged task of s is migrated from the scheduler of its originally assigned processor to the candidate scheduler (lines [14][15][16][17][18][19].

The scheduler can be fully distributed and easily scaled in implementation, since the scheduling algorithms of the uniprocessor ERD and mERD are identical except for the migration-check procedure shown in Algorithm 1.

div.head: A. Methodology and Task Sets
div.p: The evaluation methodology follows our previous study [4], with extended configurations to support up to 32 processors and multiple privileged tasks. Each processor in the system executes a statically assigned set of periodic tasks, while privileged tasks may migrate according to the mERD algorithm. In this experiment, each processor is assigned one privileged task, resulting in the same number of privileged tasks as processors.

Each task τ i is characterized by its worst-case execution time C i , period T i and deadline D i . Task utilizations were randomly generated under the constraint that the total utilization of each processor does not exceed 1.0. Specifically, tasks were added one by one with randomly assigned parameters until the utilization limit was reached; if the limit was exceeded, the generation process was restarted. Task periods were uniformly distributed within the same range as in our previous work.

For performance evaluation, we measured the response time and jitter of privileged tasks under different numbers of processors and task configurations. The proposed mERD was compared with RM, DM and partitioned ERD (pERD). In contrast, the global FTP scheduling evaluated in our previous work [4] was excluded from this study, as its schedulability significantly degrades in our use case when unrestricted migration is allowed.

All simulations were conducted using an enhanced version of the discrete-event simulator developed in our previous work. While the fundamental scheduling framework remains the same, the implementation was refined to incorporate the revised migration algorithm, improved server management, and enhanced data collection for experimental evaluation. The simulator itself imposes no limitation on the number of processors m, although the experiments in this study were conducted with up to 32 processors.
In order to create task sets of multiprocessor for RM, DM, pERD and mERD, we created partitioned task sets as follows:
• Deciding the number of processors m (m = 8, 16, 32)
• Choosing m uniprocessor task sets randomely with the same processor utilization • Assigning the m uniprocessor task sets to m processors one by one as a partitioned task set

In the experiments, m privileged tasks were selectedone for each processor -from the tasks originally assigned to that processor. Specifically, the lowest-priority task in each processor's task set was designated as the privileged task.

To raise the priority of τ pi , the following policy was applied. For DM, τ pi was assigned the shortest possible deadline while maintaining the schedulability of processor P i . For pERD, after several VS candidates were derived, the server that produced the best response-time result for τ pi was selected. For mERD, the same server configuration as in pERD was used. If multiple secondary-server (sV S) candidates were available, the first one was selected regardless of the results.

div.head: B. Results
div.p: We obtained the worst-case response time (WCRT) of each privileged task τ pi for every task set and scheduling policy. For RM and DM, the WCRT was derived analytically using RTA, whereas for pERD and mERD it was measured through discrete-event simulation. Each simulation was executed for 10,000 ticks.

Figures 7,8, and 9 show the average ratio of task sets in which the WCRT of privileged tasks τ pi was reduced compared with RM, under configurations with m = 8, m = 16, and m = 32, respectively. The horizontal axis represents the processor utilization of the task sets, and the vertical axis represents the average ratio of processors where τ pi 's WCRT was reduced relative to RM. Figures 10,11 Across all configurations, the fundamental shape and trend of the graphs remained consistent with those observed in our previous study. In every evaluated configuration, no deadline misses were observed, demonstrating that the schedulability of all task sets was maintained. The measured WCRT satisfied the relation W CRT mERD ≤ W CRT pERD ≤ W CRT DM ≤ W CRT RM confirming that mERD achieved superior timing performance while preserving feasibility.

div.head: C. Discussion
div.p: The results show that mERD maintains a stable performance trend even as the number of processors increases up to 32. This indicates that the proposed scheduling mechanism scales effectively without degradation, despite the increased number of secondary servers and privileged tasks. The primary reason for this trend is that the increase in the number of secondary servers is accompanied by a proportional increase in the number of privileged tasks. Consequently, the potential performance gain of additional migration opportunities is balanced by the increased competition among privileged tasks. In our previous study, where the number of privileged tasks was limited to two, the improvement ratio increased with the number of processors. In contrast, the extended mERD demonstrates consistent scalability when the number of privileged tasks grows with the system size.

Although the improvement ratio remained almost constant across m = 8, 16, and 32, this result indicates that mERD scales effectively with the number of processors. The increase in secondary servers provides more migration opportunities, but the concurrent increase in privileged tasks offsets additional gains. Therefore, the proposed mERD maintains stable performance without degradation, demonstrating its scalability in larger multiprocessor systems.

While mERD consistently reduced the WCRT compared with pERD, it occasionally exhibited larger jitter values. This is because the best-case response time of mERD became shorter, widening the gap between the best and worst cases. In other words, mERD achieves higher responsiveness at the cost of increased timing variability. Accordingly, the choice between the extended mERD and the previous ERD variants should depend on the system's design objective: the former is advantageous for minimizing WCRT, whereas the latter provides better timing stability with smaller jitter.

div.head: VII. CONCLUSION
div.p: This paper presented an extended version of the ERD scheduling algorithm for multiprocessor systems. The proposed mERD removes the previous limitations on the number of processors and privileged tasks, enabling each processor to host one privileged task and one secondary server. Through simulation-based evaluation, we confirmed that mERD effectively reduces the worst-case response time of privileged tasks compared with the conventional partitioned ERD and Fixed-Task-Priority scheduling. Although mERD occasionally exhibits larger jitter due to shorter best-case response time, this behavior reflects a natural trade-off between responsiveness and timing stability. Furthermore, the extended mERD demonstrated stable scalability up to 32 processors without performance degradation, indicating that the proposed scheduling framework can be applied to larger multiprocessor real-time systems. 346
